wine, and chocolate powder are especially rich sources of boron.
The Upper Intake levels (ULs) set by various ofﬁcial bodies indicate boron is a relatively nontoxic element. The United States ULs
are, for children aged 1–3 years, 3 mg day1; and aged 4–8 years, 6 mg day1. The UL for adolescents aged 9–18 years is 17 mg
day1, and for adults, 20 mg day1 (Institute of Medicine, Food and Nutrition Board, 2001). The World Health Organization, Inter-
national Program on Chemical Safety (1998) has indicated that a safe UL would be 0.4 mg kg1 body weight or 28 mg day1 for
a 70 kg person. The European Food Safety Authority (2013) established an Acceptable Daily Intake for boron at 0.16 mg day1, or
11.2 mg day1 for a 70 kg person. The past use of boric acid and borates as food preservatives provides further evidence of the low
order of toxicity for boron.
Bromine
There is evidence that indicates bromine could be considered an essential ultratrace element because a deﬁned biochemical function
that occurs in humans has been identiﬁed in Drosophila; bromide deﬁciency is lethal to Drosophila (McCall et al., 2014). Bromide has
been identiﬁed as a required co-factor for the peroxidasin-catalyzed formation of sulﬁlimine crosslinks of the collagen IV scaffold in
